subject: biology
title: Prokaryotic cells and viruses
key_idea: Prokaryotic cells such as bacteria are much smaller than eukaryotic cells and have no nucleus or membrane-bound organelles. Their DNA is circular and free in the cytoplasm. Viruses are not cells: they are non-living particles of nucleic acid in a protein coat.

blocks.text: A typical bacterium is a single cell, usually 1 to 5 µm across. It has the features of every cell, but much simpler organisation.

items: A **cell wall** made of murein (peptidoglycan), a glycoprotein, which supports the cell.
A cell surface membrane inside the wall, and cytoplasm with no membrane-bound organelles.
No nucleus. A single **circular DNA** molecule lies free in the cytoplasm and is not bound to proteins.
Smaller **70S ribosomes**, which make proteins.
No organelles surrounded by a double membrane, such as mitochondria or chloroplasts.

blocks.text: Many prokaryotic cells have extra structures.

items: **Plasmids**: small circular loops of DNA, which often carry genes such as antibiotic resistance.
A **capsule**: a slime layer outside the wall that protects the cell from drying out and from white blood cells.
One or more **flagella**, which rotate to move the cell.
**Pili**: short hair-like projections that attach the cell to surfaces and to other bacteria.
Prokaryotes: 1 to 5 µm, murein wall, circular DNA, 70S ribosomes, no organelles with a double membrane.
Plasmids, a capsule and flagella are found in many, but not all, bacteria.

blocks.text: The two cell types differ in size, in genetic material and in organelles. Mitochondria and chloroplasts are like prokaryotes: they have 70S ribosomes and circular DNA.

diagram.alt: A prokaryotic cell compared with an animal cell and a plant cell.

items: Prokaryotes are unicellular. Eukaryotes may be unicellular or multicellular.
Prokaryotes reproduce by binary fission, not mitosis.
Both types have a cell surface membrane, cytoplasm, ribosomes and DNA as genetic material.
Prokaryotes are smaller and have no nucleus, no organelles with a membrane and smaller ribosomes.
Their DNA is circular and not bound to protein.

blocks.text: Viruses are acellular and non-living. They have no cytoplasm, ribosomes or membrane, and they do not respire or grow.

items: **Genetic material**: either DNA or RNA, which forms the core.
A **capsid**: a protein coat made of repeating units that protects the nucleic acid.
**Attachment proteins**: they stick out of the particle and bind to receptors on the surface of a host cell.
Viruses can only replicate inside a living host cell, so they cannot divide by themselves.

blocks.text: A virus gets its nucleic acid into a host cell. The host cell then makes new virus particles.

rows: Circular DNA, free in the cytoplasm
DNA or RNA inside a capsid

items: A virus has a nucleic acid core, a protein capsid and attachment proteins.
Viruses are non-living and can only be replicated by a host cell.

checks.q: State three differences between a prokaryotic cell and a eukaryotic cell.
checks.a: Any three from: prokaryotic cells are smaller; have no nucleus (DNA free in the cytoplasm); have circular DNA not bound to protein; have smaller 70S ribosomes; have no membrane-bound organelles; have a murein cell wall.

checks.q: Describe the structure of a virus.
checks.a: A core of genetic material (DNA or RNA), surrounded by a protein capsid, with attachment proteins on the outside.

checks.q: Explain why viruses are described as non-living.
checks.a: They have no cells, cytoplasm or ribosomes, do not carry out metabolism, and can only replicate inside a host cell.

items: **Mesosomes** are infoldings of the cell surface membrane seen in electron micrographs. They were thought to be sites of respiration.
Many scientists now think mesosomes are artefacts produced when cells are prepared for the microscope.
**Pili** are hollow, hair-like tubes. They attach to surfaces and can pass plasmids between bacteria.
The flagellum is a rotating tail made of protein, which drives the bacterium forwards.
Bacteria are unicellular and generally 1 to 5 µm in diameter.
Some viruses have an outer **envelope** made of phospholipids, taken from the host cell membrane.
Enveloped viruses carry attachment proteins in the envelope.
All viruses have a capsid and a nucleic acid core.
